rv.q: This British version is the most merciless and empathic interpretation of this much performed work I’ve seen, and it keeps returning to my thoughts in piercing shards, like the remnants of a too-revealing dream.
Of all Pinter’s often-puzzling work, this play is the one that clearly speaks to you, thinks for you, and may even feel for you.

Aching, wistful and wounding, the director’s staging of Betrayal presents three friends and lovers trapped in an undoing of their own making, their inevitable self-destruction no less powerful for showing itself before the happier days.
And yet it also understands that infidelity has a sweet and gentle side.
It’s just six years since the last sizzling Broadway revival of this work, directed by Mike Nichols and starring Daniel Craig, Rachel Weisz and Rafe Spall, all in top form.
The three performers bring such emotional precision to Harold Pinter's reverse-chronology tale of adultery that you feel you're witnessing something profound about the nature of intimacy.
At its best, the play is white-hot. You really believe that at any moment, these gorgeous actors might rip off their clothes and do the deed.
You can feel, as I did, like you’re watching Good Actors Acting Well, which is a matter of intellect rather than emotion.
It was a strange and incongruous moment, and it provided a welcome burst of surprise in a production that is otherwise a chic and dreary affair.
Would that Mr. Lloyd's production had been able to loosen up 'Betrayal,' but it smacks of portentousness.
Bottom line: Best Broadway revival of a Harold Pinter drama in over a decade.
What could so easily come off like soap opera in lesser hands rises in this production to the level of modern tragedy.
That’s the brilliance of Lloyd’s can’t-miss revival.

There is certainly a beautiful, open elegance to Lloyd’s production that echoes its three supremely fine performances and a reading of the text that pinpoints all of Pinter’s wit, wordplay, and mordancy, while leaving a lovely breadth of interpretation open to the audience.
As Lloyd and his excellent trio of actors make devastatingly clear, the use of the singular in the title is an understatement; this is a drama rife with betrayals…
The efforts of the cast, however subtle they may be at times, are constant, rigorous, and, ultimately, brimming with potency.
The present production, thanks to Lloyd and his acting company, demonstrates that after 40 years, Pinter’s examination of truth and deception holds up exceedingly well.
All told, this is a first-rate presentation, spare perhaps in size but hardly in scope.
Lloyd strips the play to its essentials and gets at the heart of Pinter’s portrait of easy deception and the pain it causes.

Hiddleston as Robert far surpasses his most famous reputation as Loki in both Thor and The Avengers, giving a nuanced and ever-changing performance, and Cox as Jerry also finds subtleties that elude most actors, as their characters undergo constant changes.
It makes betrayal a pleasure to behold.
To borrow an art-world term, her work is “counterfeit.”
Credit for that definitely goes to Cox, in the evening's best performance, who gives Jerry a bit of a lost puppy-dog quality that goes a long way to making Robert's actions believable.
It's that kind of fogginess that finally makes this production only intermittently memorable and rarely revelatory.
Upon further study, I'm sure mountains of subtext can be excavated from each interaction, but in the moment, they offer little reason to emotionally buy in.
Despite the lingering sense that I’d witnessed the fanciest acting class in the world…getting Pinter wrong…the night is not a total loss.
The revelation for me is how little I could embrace a production so many others have admired, of a play whose subtleties I’ve appreciated in the past, and not just on paper.
The Broadway transfer of Betrayal is a powerful must-see production of a 20th-century classic that should engender as much praise in New York as it did in London.
This is the essence of this masterful revival.
This Betrayal is a quiet, balletic reflection by three players in an affair that started and ended over the course of seven years, somehow without going awry.

To Lloyd's credit, and that of this spectacular cast, we never lose sight of the ways in which these three lives are ineradicably interwoven, giving more power to the emptiness and emotional wreckage their actions have wrought – despite their best attempts to be so very British about it all.
She hardly seems worth anyone’s trouble, and I’m not sure the play does either.
In fact, the brilliance of the acting here in Jamie Lloyd’s unconventionally minimalist, finely tuned staging only serves to emphasize the play’s technical glitter over its emotional heartbeat.

tn.cat: Best Scenic Design of a Play

cn.t: Lloyd's spare, stylish revival of Pinter's reverse-chronology infidelity drama earns strong praise for its stellar cast and surgical precision, though some critics find the play itself cold and the characters unengaging despite the production's technical excellence.

vs.sum: The Bernard B. Jacobs Theatre offers excellent sightlines from most seats, though comfort is compromised by tight legroom, especially in the mezzanine. The theater's ambiance is enhanced by its historic architecture and unique murals, but restroom facilities are limited, leading to long lines during intermission.

acc.note: 7 wheelchair spaces in Orchestra. Copper induction loop available.
